newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica seeks international help for Kabila's Congo.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica seeks international help for Kabila's Congo.

text.p: South Africa called on Thursday for an Africa-led international effort to help rebuild the shattered economy of Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad, fresh from a two-day visit to Kinshasa, said urgent help was needed for the vast and mineral-rich former Zaire.

"The challenge facing the Democratic Republic of the Congo can only be successfully met if there is a coordinated international effort to assist the country...This effort must be an African-led initiative," Pahad told a news conference on the return from Kinshasa of a South African delegation.
Pahad said the country, crippled by over three decades of corrupt rule under ousted leader Mobutu Sese Seko, was in dire need of quick help.
"The clear message that is coming through is that we must act very quickly and urgently on an overall programme."

The South African visit, which included officials from the Reserve Bank and the Finance Ministry, was aimed at providing technical advice to self-appointed President Kabila as he seeks to govern the country he won control of in a lightning seven-month civil war.
The South Africans met Kabila and Pahad said his new government appeared strongly committed to development.

No firm plan of assistance had yet emerged but Pahad said the first areas Kabila aimed to target included infrastructure development, reforming the central bank, launching a new currency and promoting industrialisation -- mainly in manufacturing and mining.
Kabila's fledgling government has already signed up America Mineral Fields Inc to develop the Kolwezi copper/cobalt tailings project and build a 200,000 tonne-a-year zinc plant at Kipushi.
A host of other foreign firms are also licking their lips at the prospect of tapping into the country's enormous and largely undeveloped resources.
Pahad said companies, especially South African firms, should start moving in soon or risk missing the boat to an investment bonanza.
"If they hesitate, it will be a hesitation to their own loss," he said.
Pahad said one area of concern would be working out how to deal with the crippling burden of $14 billion in debt inherited from Mobutu's era.
Earlier on Thursday the World Bank pledged support for Kabila's government and said it would hold a meeting of donors for the country by September.

Kabila's battlefield victory was broadly welcomed by the world community, but a U.N. investigation team is expected to look into the alleged massacre of thousands of Rwandan Hutus by his forces and their regional allies.
Kabila has denied any killings took place or that he ordered officials to obstruct the U.N. team.
Pahad said Kabila had pledged full cooperation with the investigation.
"We don't want to prejudge it. Let's wait for a report from the U.N. agencies," he added.
The key to ending the spiral of violence in Central Africa in the past few years was political stability and economic development.
To this end Pahad said he would welcome any application from Kabila's Congo to join the Southern African Development Community, which groups Zaire's southern neighbours.
"Clearly it makes good sense if they make such an application... I believe it will strengthen SADC," he said.
